data.title: Pružina – Mesciská, a hillfort described as early as 1856
data.excerpt: Two adjoining rampart circuits on a limestone promontory above the hamlet of Riedka were first described in 1856 by Anton Intibus, one of the first Slovak archaeologists – and then forgotten for almost 150 years. A hoard of 9th-century iron objects found here is, in the words of Dr Karol Pieta, the largest Slavic hoard in Slovakia.
data.metaTitle: Pružina – Mesciská: a hillfort described back in 1856
data.metaDescription: Two rampart circuits above the hamlet of Riedka, described in 1856 and then forgotten for 150 years. The hoard found here is Slovakia’s largest Slavic one.

keyFacts.label: Total area
keyFacts.value: approximately 2.6 ha (Mesciská I – 2.03 ha, Mesciská II – 0.58 ha)

keyFacts.label: Location
keyFacts.value: A rocky limestone promontory at the confluence of the Mojtínsky and Strážovský streams above the hamlet of Riedka, the ground rising some 20–25 m above the streams

keyFacts.label: Two separate fortifications
keyFacts.value: The hillfort consists of two parts, Mesciská I and Mesciská II, separated by a deeper gully

keyFacts.label: Rampart dimensions
keyFacts.value: The rampart of Mesciská I is 260 m long, 3–4 m wide at the crown and 1.5–7 m high; the circuit of the hillfort measures 611 m

keyFacts.label: Archaeological finds
keyFacts.value: Slavic, Púchov-culture and La Tène sherds, traces of iron slag by the eastern gateway and possible remains of a charred palisade below the slope

keyFacts.label: A Great Moravian hoard
keyFacts.value: A hoard found at the hillfort holds at least 4 riding stirrups, 8 spurs, axe-shaped currency bars, axes, keys, horse bits and agricultural tools of the 9th century – according to Dr Karol Pieta the largest Slavic hoard in Slovakia

keyFacts.label: A forgotten discovery
keyFacts.value: Anton Intibus’s article of 1856 went unnoticed by scholars for almost 150 years

keyFacts.label: Local legends
keyFacts.value: Legend links the neighbouring crag of Pivničenská skala with outlaws’ treasure and with a Turkish suspension bridge of leather straps across a flooded Riedka

children.text: The first to write about the so-called Pružina enclosure (the Pružina ramparts) was Anton Intibus in 1856, one of the first Slovak archaeologists. Of Mesciská he writes the following: “…

beyond the village of Pružiná, upon the boundary betwixt the districts of Čičmany and Tŕstie, above Chmelisko – a hamlet made up of a few hovels – there rise, hard by the said Mlýnisko, prehistoric settlements named Městisko.”

His article, however, went unnoticed by scholars for almost 150 years and his discovery literally fell into oblivion. Only in the late 1990s, during a survey by members of the archaeological circle of the Matica slovenská local branch (MO MS) in Považská Bystrica led by Š. Meliš, was this rampart fortification in the cadastral area of the village of Pružina rediscovered. The find was then verified by the archaeologists Dr Moravčík and Dr Pieta, who carried out a field inspection.

This is the fortification of a rocky limestone promontory at the confluence of the Mojtínsky and Strážovský streams, on which the isolated settlement of Riedka lies. It takes the form of two enclosed rampart circuits separated by a deeper gully. The ground rises some 20–25 metres above the level of the streams. The interior is covered in small part by woodland and mostly by meadows. According to the survey made by its discoverers, the hillfort complex covers an area of about 2.6 ha (2.03 + 0.58 ha). Prominent and well-preserved rampart banks lie along the edges of the plateau above the steep slopes. The southern rampart of the larger enclosure is of monumental proportions. Of the four present-day openings, the western entrance appears to be the original gateway, for here the rampart bank is slightly thickened and projects partly outwards.

Several Slavic sherds dated to the 9th century, that is to the period of the existence of Great Moravia, were found at the hillfort. Others belonged to the Púchov culture of the Late La Tène period. In addition, production features were identified, attested by finds of iron slag by the eastern rampart not far from the eastern gateway of the defences. Massive ramparts enclose the larger of the two fortifications here, with a total area of about 2.03 ha. Dr Moravčík stated that even after repeated test trenching across the whole area of the fortification no occupation layer could be identified at the time of the evaluation excavation. For this reason the hillfort is, at the present state of research, regarded rather as a refuge, without continuous and above all longer-term occupation. The Slavic ancestors of today’s inhabitants of Pružina thus probably built the hillfort (or rather renewed it in the Early Middle Ages) so as to have somewhere to take shelter from the enemy in time of danger. The use of the hillfort may be connected with the Magyar incursions into the northern Váh region or with attacks by other hostile forces in the 9th and 10th centuries.

There are several important archaeological sites in the vicinity of the hillfort. Above the valley rises the massif of the hill Stráža (cadastral area of Tŕstie) with a Púchov-culture hillfort. The fortification is, however, more closely linked to a concentration of Slavic occupation (Beluša-Pechová, Beluša-Pod Malenicou) with nearby barrow cemeteries in the cadastral areas of the villages of Beluša, Visolaje, Sverepec and Dolný Lieskov. An important hoard of iron objects of the Great Moravian period is said to come from the area of the hillfort, but so far I have not managed to obtain photographs of it from the Institute of Archaeology of the Slovak Academy of Sciences in Nitra.

With the kind permission of Mr Martin Olšovský, Štefan Meliš and Jozef Moravčík – members of the former archaeological circle in Považská Bystrica – we bring you their 1996 report on the investigation of the hillfort. It is an amateur, not an official, excavation report, yet the quality of its treatment is of a high standard. The report appeared in an exceptional collection of documents and photographs entitled Po stopách predkov, Archeológia Stredného Považia od praveku po stredovek (In the Footsteps of Our Ancestors: The Archaeology of the Middle Váh Region from Prehistory to the Middle Ages), published at his own expense by Mr Martin Olšovský in 2008 in a print run of 4 copies.
“THE MESCISKÁ HILLFORT
(Report on the investigation by the Archaeol. Circle of the MOMS in Považská Bystrica )

Date: 14 July 1996 Aim: - Surveying, sketching and preliminary investigation of the hillfort above the hamlet of Riedka in the cadastral area of the village of Pružina. - Establishing the available data on the site, gathering information on notable finds, sites and legends from the surrounding area
The investigation was undertaken at the suggestion of Mr Ľudovít Berhan of Považská Bystrica
Participants: Štefan Meliš, Ing. Vojtech Miko, Vincent Krivý, Martin Olšovský.

children.text: Facts established:
I. The M E S C I S K Á hillfort

The hillfort lies on a promontory spur of the hill Svrčinovec above the confluence of the Mojtínsky and Strážovský streams, immediately above the hamlet of Riedka (Ritka) in the cadastral area of the village of Pružina, Považská Bystrica district. The owners of the land within the site cannot explain the name of the site – Mesciská (Mrs Alžbeta Kozáková, aged 88, and her son Alojz Kozák, aged 42). The name is probably derived from the word “mesto” (town) - in dialect “dve veľké mestá” (two large towns) = mesciská, in our case two settlements, two hillforts side by side. The hillfort is in fact made up of two relatively independent units:
Mesciská I:

The larger of the two hillforts, on the NE side of a terrace sloping gently to the NW, has an outer circuit of 611 m and an area of approximately 2.03 ha. On the NW, SW and SE sides the defences consist of a massive continuous rampart 260 m long, 3–4 m wide at the crown and 1.5–7 m high (1). A lower above-ground rampart about 20 m long also runs in the N spur of the hillfort (2). On the SE outer side of the rampart there is a shallow ditch (0.8-1 m), 2.5–3 m wide and 90 m long (3). A smaller ditch flanks the rampart for about 30 m on the inner side as well, in the W arc of the defences (4). The remaining circuit of the hillfort, some 330 m long, is formed by the edge of the plateau with steep rocky slopes. This natural rampart is strengthened in several places on the NW and NE sides with small stone retaining walls (5,6,7). The defences are interrupted at 4 points (probably entrance gateways), where tracks that are still clearly recognisable come out (8,9,10,11). In the SE part of the hillfort, now wooded, there are three stepped terraces, probably an acropolis (12). By the SW arc of the rampart there is a remarkable spot: - elongated openings of approximately 8x20 cm and also larger rectangular openings about 15x60 cm in size have been cut into a rock measuring about 3x2x0.7 m. The position of this spot within the site and the working of the natural rock outcrop may point to a cult place - a sacrificial site? (13). In the central part of the hillfort there are two larger heaps of undressed stone of local origin (14,15). According to the informants (the owners of the land) this is stone cleared from the cultivated plots. From the position of the stone heaps within the area of the hillfort it may be inferred that the foundations of hillfort or sacred buildings lie beneath them. Most of the area of the hillfort (apart from the wooded SE part) is covered with tall grass, which hampers test trenching. For this reason too, direct finds are so far sparse: on the steep NE slope, close to the edge of the defences, Š. Meliš found a non-diagnostic sherd of Púchov pottery (16), on the surface a non-diagnostic La Tène graphite sherd (17), a sherd from the rim of a Slavic vessel - 9th cent. (18), a typical Slavic sherd with a fine groove and a wavy line (19) and a non-diagnostic Slavic sherd (20). The sherds, together with daub and burnt stones (?), were found shallowly below the surface in the humic layer. An informant reported that below the NE slope in the valley, during the digging of a trench for a water main, thick charred beams were found at a depth of about 2 m, protruding from the boggy subsoil - preserved remains of a palisade? (21). During the cultivation of the plots within the area of the hillfort a complete pottery vessel was reportedly found, but they can give no details about it or about the circumstances of the find. The informants associate the site with the Turks (not, however, in connection with the hillfort, which they do not mention at all, but with treasure supposedly hidden there - probably at location 13).

children.text: Mesciská II:

This part of the site is considerably smaller: - circuit 305 m, area about 0.58 ha. It lies in the SW spur of the terrace. The division of the hillfort into two parts was probably caused by the configuration of the terrain: - torrential water pouring off the N slope of Svrčinovec evidently damaged the rampart in the part where the Berhanovci farmstead now stands (22). The level upper surface of the hillfort was created artificially. On the W and NW it is protected by steep rocky slopes; the NE side was of earth, and so today it has spread out into a gentle slope (23). On the SE side, towards the hill, the plateau is protected by a prominent rampart (width 3–4 m, height 1–1.5), 70 m long (24), ending on the W side in a projection - a tower, a gateway? (25). Behind it a track clearly runs out from the corner of the hillfort (26). A similar projection is also present in the opposite corner of the defences, above the gully separating the two hillforts (27). On the E side the rampart is cut off vertically by the rear wall of a farm building. The whole area of the hillfort is covered with grass. No finds are known as yet.

Conclusion: From the advantageous position, the imposing area (2.61 ha in all) and the massive defences it may be concluded that this is one of the most important hillforts of NW Slovakia. The modest finds do not yet allow the time span of the occupation to be determined more precisely, but La Tène, Púchov and Slavic occupation may be assumed, and occupation of the hillforts in the Middle Ages cannot be ruled out either - indeed the name Mesciská positively suggests it. Other find spots in the hamlet of Riedka:

In the area between the Makyty Púchov chalet and the little waterworks below the wood, about 100 m south of the chalet, human skulls and, beside them, complete small vessels, finely made and smooth, were reportedly found about 30 years ago during the digging of a water-main trench. Human skulls were also found during the digging of the foundations of the forester’s lodge about 120 m NW of the chalet and 20 m from the lodge in the direction of Chmelisko.
Legends obtained from informants:
Pivničenská(outlaws’) skala.

A crag about 15 m high opposite the hamlet of Riedka, the end of the Stráža massif. It is said to conceal the mysterious treasure of outlaws; in a deep pit - a cellar - demons, evil forces harmful to people, are said to lurk. A brief survey showed that the legends had a preventive and educational purpose: - to stop children climbing the dangerous steep rocks, easily reached from Stráža by a path.

Another legend connected with Pivničenská skala says that in olden times Riedka was flooded by the waters of a natural lake formed by the blocking of the narrows near the quarry between Riedka and Tŕstie. The Turks are said to have built a suspension bridge of leather straps from the hillfort to the crag of Pivničenská skala, by which they crossed the water obstacle.
In Považská Bystrica, 4.8.1996
Recorded by: Martin Olšovský Head of the circle: Štefan Meliš”

And finally one piece of current news. A hoard was found at the hillfort – that is, a mass find of a quantity of astonishing iron objects which can broadly be dated to the 9th century, that is to the period of the existence of Great Moravia, or possibly still to the period of the Principality of Nitra. The find includes at least 4 very well-preserved riding stirrups, 8 spurs, a large quantity of Great Moravian currency – axe-shaped currency bars – axes, keys, horse bits, agricultural tools and many other objects. The find has not yet been officially published; according to a statement made to our website by Dr Karol Pieta, it is our largest Slavic hoard. This find will evidently revise the previous understanding of the Pružina hillfort as merely a minor refuge, and its greater importance in the period of Great Moravia will probably come to be considered.

I should also like to ask the inhabitants of Pružina to contact me by e-mail if they have found an interesting object at the hillfort in the past.
